chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Ibrahim ibn Is'haq al-Ahmar, from Abdullah ibn Hammad, from Umar ibn Yazeed, who said:

A man came to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) to ask for payment/help, and I was present. He (peace be upon him) said to him: 'We do not have anything with us today, but a shipment (khitr) and a brand of camels (wasima) will come to us, so we will sell them and give you, God willing.' The man said to him, 'Promise me.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'How can I promise you what I am hoping for, when I am more hopeful of what I am expecting than you are of what you are expecting from me?'

key_terms.خِطْرٌ: a shipment or consignment of goods (specifically camels or livestock in this context)
key_terms.وَسِمَةٌ: a brand or mark on camels, referring to a specific group of branded camels
key_terms.يَقْتَضِيهِ: to claim a debt or payment from someone

ai.seo_question: How did Imam al-Sadiq handle a debt claim when funds were not immediately available?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the Imam’s practical approach to debt fulfillment, emphasizing that sincere hope and certainty in divine provision serve as a valid guarantee when immediate liquidity is absent. The rhetorical question underscores the Shia scholarly principle that the Imam’s confidence in receiving the 'khitran' (likely a specific commodity or shipment) reflects a spiritual and economic trustworthiness that reassures the creditor. It highlights the balance between transparency about current lack of funds and the assurance of future payment based on expected revenue.
